MASLD is increasingly framed not as an isolated hepatic diagnosis but as one node within a broader cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic (CKLM) or cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome that also encompasses type 2 diabetes, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), hypertension, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [@QuirinoVela2026The]. A structured narrative synthesis proposes a "unified cardiometabolic disease" continuum in which visceral adipose tissue dysfunction, ceramide-mediated lipotoxicity, NF-κB/NLRP3-driven inflammation, gut-derived endotoxemia and TMAO, adipokine dysregulation, and a cardiorenal amplification loop drive progression across all of these phenotypes, with stage-specific mediators serving as candidate biomarkers [@QuirinoVela2026The]. This framing is reinforced by epidemiologic data showing that MASLD, now affecting more than one-third of adults worldwide, coexists with CKD and cardiovascular disease and independently predicts kidney function decline, cardiovascular events, and mortality, yet remains underrecognized in nephrology and cardiology practice [@Tsai2026Metabolic]. A parallel "dual-heart-liver" model highlights bidirectional epidemiologic and mechanistic links between MASLD and coronary artery disease—endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, insulin resistance, and shared genetic susceptibility—and calls for systematic cardiovascular risk assessment in every MASLD patient [@Zhu2026Heartliver]. Obesity-driven complications extend further still, encompassing obstructive sleep apnea, dyslipidemia, and obesity-related glomerulopathy mediated by renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation and glomerular hyperfiltration [@Bracale2026Cardiometabolic], against a backdrop of a global obesity epidemic that has nearly tripled in prevalence since 1975 and now underpins cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, and oncologic disease burden worldwide [@Henney2026The]. Traditional and emerging predictors of incident ASCVD in patients with type 2 diabetes and MASLD are being reassessed within this same continuum [@Vulpescu2026Traditional], and state-of-the-art reviews increasingly frame MASLD pharmacotherapy selection around this complication-centric, multisystem model rather than liver-only endpoints [@Chan2026Pharmacological; @Li2026Liver].

Within this CKM framework, GLP-1 receptor agonists and tirzepatide are increasingly positioned against or alongside other cardiometabolic agents. Fibrates, reappraised through the CKLM lens, activate PPAR-α and show the strongest evidence for slowing diabetic retinopathy progression, with post hoc signals for reduced albuminuria/eGFR decline and only modest hepatic benefit from fenofibrate—positioning fibrates as a complement to, not a substitute for, incretin-based therapy for residual microvascular risk [@Anagnostopoulou2026Therapies]. Head-to-head comparisons with SGLT2 inhibitors are accumulating rapidly. In a propensity-matched retrospective study, subcutaneous GLP-1RAs produced superior HbA1c and BMI reduction versus SGLT2 inhibitors (β = -0.349, p = 0.001; β = -0.711, p = 0.045) and were the only class associated with significant ALT reduction in patients with elevated baseline ALT or hepatic steatosis (p = 0.02), with the GLP1R rs761387 variant identified as an independent predictor of blunted glycemic response [@Toffoli2026Comparative]. A large TriNetX-based propensity-matched cohort comparing semaglutide (n = 128,332) with SGLT2 inhibitors (n = 100,542) found semaglutide associated with markedly lower 1-year hazards of mortality (HR 0.382), hospitalization (HR 0.444), MACE (HR 0.502), and major adverse liver outcomes (HR 0.361), with attenuated but persistent benefit at 5 years [@Khalil2026Efficacy]. A German claims-based cohort of 45,256 people with MASLD and type 2 diabetes similarly found GLP-1RA use associated with a lower hazard of major adverse liver outcomes versus SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 0.91, strengthening to HR 0.78 on-treatment), including reduced cirrhosis (HR 0.88) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HR 0.76), though without a difference in all-cause mortality [@Maier2026GlucagonLike]. Target trial emulations using TriNetX further suggest GLP-1RA plus SGLT2i combination therapy reduces mortality (corrected HR 0.655) and composite liver outcomes (corrected HR 0.907) versus SGLT2i monotherapy, but carries increased MACE risk versus GLP-1RA monotherapy alone (corrected HR 1.111)—a trade-off relevant to sequencing [@Alkuwaiti2026GLP]. A network meta-analysis of 34 histologic MASH trials found SGLT2 inhibitors numerically outperforming GLP-1RAs for fibrosis improvement (RR 2.27 vs RR 1.51), with FGF21 analogues (RR 2.22) and GLP-1/GIP dual agonists (RR 5.21 for resolution) ranking highest overall—underscoring that GLP-1RA monotherapy is not the top-performing agent on every histologic endpoint even as it remains foundational for cardiometabolic risk reduction [@Tang2026Updating; @Mahoon2026Therapeutic].

A distinct evidentiary gap concerns metabolic and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD), an emerging phenotype combining cardiometabolic risk factors with concurrent alcohol exposure that produces synergistic liver injury and faster fibrosis progression. Because most MASLD trials exclude patients with ongoing alcohol use and alcohol-associated liver disease trials focus on severe alcoholic hepatitis, dedicated MetALD evidence is essentially absent, forcing clinicians to extrapolate from both literatures. Current management integrates alcohol-use control—prioritized as the dominant driver given its faster disease trajectory, using acamprosate or naltrexone alongside psychosocial intervention—with cardiometabolic therapies including incretin-based agents, FGF21 analogues, PPAR agonists, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists in selected patients, plus longitudinal noninvasive fibrosis monitoring given the dynamic nature of both exposures [@Pagadala2026Pharmacologic].

Special clinical contexts further shape GLP-1RA positioning. In inflammatory bowel disease, more than half of patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis are overweight or obese at diagnosis, and visceral adipose tissue—independent of BMI—drives disease activity, reduced therapeutic response, and surgical risk while amplifying comorbid MASLD and cardiovascular disease. Preclinical data show GLP-1RAs reduce visceral adiposity, modulate gut microbiota, and attenuate proinflammatory signaling relevant to IBD pathogenesis, and emerging human data suggest GLP-1RA therapy is safe in IBD and associated with lower hospitalization and surgical risk, though effects on luminal disease activity remain unclear, warranting multidisciplinary care attentive to GI tolerability and lean mass loss [@BeniwalPatel2026The]. Gastroenterologists are also increasingly central to peri-procedural GLP-1RA management: because these agents slow gastric emptying, they raise the incidence of retained gastric contents and procedural disruption at endoscopy, yet real-world data show no increase in aspiration pneumonia among GLP-1RA users undergoing colonoscopy (approximately 0.01%-0.05%) and only a small absolute rise in aspiration-related events during upper endoscopy (fewer than 0.3% of procedures). Contemporary guidance therefore favors continuing GLP-1RA therapy with structured risk assessment, selective point-of-care gastric ultrasound, and a pre-procedural clear liquid diet rather than routine cessation [@Beig2026GLP], consistent with gastroenterologists' expanding role across obesity medicine, GLP-1 therapy, and metabolic care [@Alali2026Beyond].

Cirrhosis management in patients with diabetes presents distinct pharmacologic constraints. As MASLD becomes the dominant driver of cirrhosis, hepatogenous diabetes complicates diagnosis (HbA1c loses reliability in advanced liver disease) and treatment: metformin remains first-line in compensated cirrhosis, GLP-1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors show promise specifically in compensated disease with cardiorenal comorbidity, sulfonylureas and fluid-retaining agents require caution as hepatic reserve declines, and insulin remains the cornerstone once decompensation or hospitalization occurs, with conservative titration to avoid hypoglycemia [@Kumar2026Management]. National guidelines echo this stepwise approach, recommending GLP-1RA consideration in eligible patients with type 2 diabetes or obesity while reserving multidisciplinary management, HCC surveillance, and transplant evaluation for decompensated cirrhosis [@Zerem2026Clinical; @Chianetta2026Emerging]. Trial evidence in compensated cirrhosis remains disappointing overall: a phase 2 trial testing zalfermin combined with semaglutide in participants with F2-F4c fibrosis (including compensated cirrhosis) found the combination did not significantly improve fibrosis without MASH worsening versus placebo (24% vs 16%; p = 0.19), though semaglutide alone showed a nominally significant effect (30% vs 16%; p = 0.024), suggesting semaglutide alone—rather than combination strategies—merits further evaluation in this population [@Loomba2026Efficacy]. This mirrors a broader pattern across MASH-cirrhosis drug development in which most investigational agents have failed to show clear histologic benefit, with FGF21 analogues currently the most promising class and GLP-1/glucagon dual agonists among several approaches still advancing [@Zeng2026Drug].

GLP-1RAs also carry a dual-edged relationship with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk. Real-world studies and target trial emulations suggest GLP-1RA use is associated with lower rates of hepatic decompensation, cirrhosis progression, and incident HCC, with the strongest apparent benefit observed against insulin or sulfonylureas and attenuated differences versus other metabolically favorable comparators such as SGLT2 inhibitors—consistent with the HCC hazard ratio of 0.76 reported in the German MASLD-diabetes cohort—though effects in established cirrhosis appear less consistent and causality remains unproven [@Vozza2026GLP; @Maier2026GlucagonLike]. Finally, as multi-receptor agonism advances toward glucagon receptor co-activation, cardiovascular safety within this CKM population warrants scrutiny: GCGR/GLP-1 dual agonists such as mazdutide and survodutide raise heart rate to a degree similar to cardioprotective GLP-1 monoagonists while also lowering blood pressure and glycemia, but at least one dual agonist was discontinued for excessive heart-rate increases and QTc prolongation, and compound-specific effects are being clarified in dedicated outcomes trials including SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT [@Kushner2026Cardiovascular].
